title: The Boasting of the Gospel and the Conscience
english: On 2 Corinthians 1:1: When he reproached them before, he did not reproach them alone; and now that he is making peace, he does not write alone either. By taking holy Timothy as his partner he shows that the matter can be trusted. Here he also showed that “through” belongs to the Father as well, when he said “through the will of God.”

The second catena form adds: Since he says “from God our Father,” we should know that with respect to those who are born he is called both God and Father, but with respect to the Son he is Father only. For Christ said “my God and your God” while he was in the flesh (John 20:17).

On 2 Corinthians 1:3: The glory he gives to God and the titles he uses for him already announce the coming reconciliation. “Father of mercies and God of all comfort”: with respect to those who are born he is called both God and Father, but with respect to the Son he is confessed as Father only. To people in affliction it is fitting that he opens with God's mercies and comfort, letting good hopes show through; for if God is the Father of mercies, he would comfort those who are persecuted and afflicted for his sake.

On 2 Corinthians 1:4: When God comforts and consoles, his consolation is not a small thing. Paul announces this in advance because he was about to call back, by this comfort, the man condemned for his sin.

On 2 Corinthians 1:6: Our affliction turns into your consolation; for if the apostles suffer affliction, how much more the rest. Or he means this: if men afflict us for the sake of your salvation, we suffer it because we preach Christ to you. And if God consoles us on your account, it is so that we may be equal to encouraging you, and so urge you to bear the same sufferings that we endure.
On 2 Corinthians 1:7: I hope that you who endure the same things as I do will receive comfort from God just as I do.
On 2 Corinthians 1:8: He tells of the afflictions that came on him in Asia, not to show off, but to anoint them for enduring their sufferings. The phrase means: so that we gave up even on living.

On 2 Corinthians 1:9: A “sentence” is the verdict that a judgment delivers. So, as far as it lay with us, we had received the verdict of death. It brings us to our senses, so that we trust not in ourselves but in God, who saves even those who have given themselves up for lost.

On 2 Corinthians 1:11: He does not pray to escape those plotting against him because he loves his body. He prays so that he may serve the gifts given to him, and so that many people now, and many still to come, may give thanks for the preaching that keeps them safe. By saying “through many,” he pointed to the teaching that will reach those still to come. And “thanks may be given on your behalf” stands for “for the gift that we ourselves have also received.”

On 2 Corinthians 1:12: Our boast is this: our conscience testifies that we preach rightly. He holds that the wisdom of outsiders is merely natural, and here he hints that he did not speak as outsiders do. Nor did he preach for a fleshly motive, such as getting something from them.

On 2 Corinthians 1:13–14: What we taught you when we were with you is no different from what we write now. It is the very same, and you read it without ornament. From this you can tell that our speech is untrained, while the power that works for faith belongs to God. Paul calls the Corinthians his boast because of what he achieved by preaching to them; and on the day of Christ he is the Corinthians' own boast, since they will have glory, so to speak, for receiving the preaching. I hope you will come to see, as in part you already see, that on the day of the Lord we are your boast as you are ours. Preachers take pride in what their preaching achieved, and believers take honor in having believed it.
